children: Butt Bridge is a road bridge across the Liffey that joins George’s Quay to Beresford Place. The bridge was a structural steel swivel bridge, opened in 1879. It was named for the leader of the Home Rule Movement Isaac Butt who died that year. The swing section, made of wrought iron and weighing approximately 200 tons, ran on a series of cast spoke wheels and was powered by a steam engine, which was housed on a timber pier on the downstream side of the bridge. The swing action allowed boats to pass and berth in the river as far upstream as O'Connell Bridge.

children: We learn that a night watchman named Gumley was a member of the Invincibles Gang that murdered the Chief Secretary and Under-Secretary on May 6, 1882 (22 years prior to Bloomsday) in Phoenix Park.
In Chapter 12 “Cylops”
we learn that Gumley was sued by Reuben J. Dodd for not paying a debt but the Recorder hears his hard luck story and dismisses the case.
Shortly after 1:00 A.M. Stephen
spots Gumley in a watchman’s sentry-box in Chapter 16 Eumaeus. He knows that he is a friend of his fathers but avoids his detection.
There was no chance that Stephen would be detected because
Bloom sees that Gumley is asleep on the job.
A little later,

a street noise wakes the dozing night watchman and we learn that in spite of once having a decent income, he is a “broken down” alcoholic and nearly broke. It appears that he has been given the watchman’s job out of charity.
Gumley is still asleep When Bloom and Stephen emerge from the cabman’s shelter and head for Bloom’s house.
Bloom thinks that it is appropriate that the ex-revolutionary is asleep on the job and “guarding” stones.

“Robert Altman’s films may be most easily recognized through the director’s unique approach to dialogue.  Rather than utilizing the more traditional give-and-take approach to a conversation, Altman would have two, three, or even entire rooms full of people delivering their lines at the same time.  This overlapping dialogue, while unconventional and often difficult to comprehend, created a sense of realism that became a staple of Altman’s films.  Altman never seemed to be overly concerned with creating a digestible piece of cinema–he recreated life and dropped us right in the middle of it.  We do not simply view a Robert Altman picture, we experience it in full immersion.”
